That demonstrates reliable large-scale renewable electricity isn’t just theoretical.

Also, nuclear power is a key low-carbon alternative that can help finish the switch faster: compared with many renewable options, it can supply large amounts of steady power with far less land, reducing the time and space barriers to ending fossil fuel dependence. The combination of proven renewable systems plus nuclear makes a full replacement feasible rather than speculative.

In the U.S., alternative energy use has never exceeded about 20% historically, which suggests renewables haven’t been able to cover a large fraction of total energy demand (including transport and industry) in practice, not just for electricity.

Also, the proposed “fast replacement” overlooks the bridging need for a controllable fossil fuel. Natural gas—an existing resource and compatible with current infrastructure—can rapidly cut emissions compared with coal while renewables, grid upgrades, storage, and demand-side systems are built out. That makes it a realistic path to net-zero.

Finally, agent 1 positions nuclear as a helpful accelerator, but nuclear is not a serious global-warming solution given the severe risk of catastrophic accidents (e.g., Fukushima) and the practical barriers and delays that come with building and maintaining plants. Those risks erase much of the benefit of low-carbon electricity.

So: renewables are part of the mix, but the idea that they can “effectively replace” fossil fuels anytime soon is unrealistic; natural gas as a bridge fuel is necessary to achieve net-zero on a workable timeline.
